MPP tracking (normalized) data under same Page 38 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology Project 7: Modeling Techniques to Screen Novel Perovskite Formulations for Improved PV Performance Our first work explored physics-based models as we detailed in Brenes et al. (Phys. Rev. Applied 12, 014017 (2019)). Briefly, the model considers losses due to bulk Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) and Auger recombination, as well as incorporating gains due to photon recycling. This helps to assess the maximum potential power-conversion efficiency (PCE) for perovskite thin films. In Fig. 7.1 we show fits the two intensity-dependent TRPL data collected on FAPb(IxBr1-x)3 films passivated with hexylammonium bromide. Through the recombination rate constants extracted from these fits, we determined that these passivated films have a maximum potential PCE ~28% while the devices have achieved maximum efficiencies of ~25%, indicating small amounts of loss due to the presence of either transport loss during charge extraction or interfacial recombination. Figure 7.1. Intensity dependent TRPL data taken at carrier densities 1014 cm-3 (blue), 1015 cm-3 (orange) and 1016 cm-3 (green). The solid lines represent fits to the data using a rate equation considering SRH, radiative and Auger recombination. This initial model has limitations for predicting the actual device operation, since it does not incorporate interfacial recombination between layers in the solar cell stack, band-bending at interfaces and internal electric fields developed due to the charge extraction layers and charge transport losses. These non-idealities could be included using a drift-diffusion model and using fits to experimental data to determine the relevant simulation parameters. Nevertheless, the number of free parameters in these models require extensive measurements and fitting models that hinders their usefulness as a predictive tool. Therefore, we began exploring the use of machine learning to take the measured physical parameters of the perovskite layers within a solar cell structure as input to directly predict the JV curve, thereby predicting the cell efficiency performance. These “Blackbox models” allow us to potentially predict the performance of full devices with data that might contain many physical processes that could be too complex to predict accurately with an analytical model.
